title: A full hotel, one more guest
hook: Every room is taken, and the rooms never run out. Where does the new guest sleep?

knows: that with more people than boxes, two must share (pigeonhole)
doesNotKnow: that an infinite collection can make room for one more without losing anyone

misconception: A full hotel is full, even if it has infinitely many rooms.
objective: The learner can explain that moving the guest in room n to room n + 1 frees room 1 and leaves nobody out, because every room has a next room; in a 12-room hotel the same move leaves someone without a room.

claims.text: If the guest in room n moves to room n + 1 for every n, every guest still has a room, no two share, and room 1 is empty.
claims.source: The map n -> n + 1 on the positive whole numbers is one-to-one and every value is a room (there is always a room n + 1); no n maps to 1.

claims.text: In a hotel with 12 rooms the same move leaves guest 12 with no room 13.
claims.source: Rooms 1..12 only; n -> n + 1 sends 12 to 13, which does not exist. More guests (13) than rooms (12) forces someone out (pigeonhole).

claims.text: With infinitely many rooms, 'full' does not mean 'no space': this is Hilbert's hotel, a thought experiment about infinite sets, not a real building.
claims.source: Attributed to David Hilbert's 1924 lectures, popularised by George Gamow, 'One Two Three... Infinity' (1947).

recall.question: An endless row of seats, numbered 1, 2, 3, ..., is completely full. Two more people arrive. Can they sit without anyone leaving?
options: Yes: everyone moves up two seats
recall.why: Moving the person in seat n to seat n + 2 frees seats 1 and 2, and everyone still has a seat because there is always a seat n + 2.
